name: AD744 / AD746 (precision 500 ns-settling BiFET single / dual)
tagline: ADI's c.1990 fast-settling JFET-input single/dual, pitched by ADI for audio (0.0003% THD), now best known as the die found inside fake OPA627s.
technology: BiFET (JFET-input) op-amp by Analog Devices. ADI describes the AD744 as having the DC characteristics of the AD711 BiFET family with faster settling, slew and bandwidth. The AD744 single has an external compensation/decompensation pin and offset-null pins. The AD746 dual is two AD744 amplifiers on one chip (ADI datasheet wording) and has no compensation pin. The AD744 datasheet lists plastic mini-DIP, SOIC, cerdip, TO-99 metal can and chip (bare die) form. Datasheet titles: "Precision, 500 ns Settling BiFET Op Amp" (AD744) and "Dual Precision, 500 ns Settling, BiFET Op Amp" (AD746).

reputation.summary: A niche part for Hi-Fi hobbyists. ADI itself pitched the AD744 for demanding audio applications (0.0003% THD, 13 MHz GBW) and as a fast-settling buffer for 12/14-bit DACs and ADCs. Tangent's CMoy op-amp survey (read via the Soomal translation) measured the AD744: $4.52 at Digi-Key, minimum supply 6.8 V for 0.5 V into 33 ohms; no listening verdict was found. Its main notoriety is as the donor die in counterfeit OPA627s (ZeptoBars, April 2014, covered by Hackaday, Head-Fi and diyAudio). The discovery note calling it a '1990s DIY I/V favourite' has no primary community source.
typical_uses: Fast-settling buffers for 12/14-bit DACs and ADCs (ADI positioning)
DAC I/V and line stages (discovery note; not verified)
caveats: The AD744's compensation pin has no counterpart on the OPA627 (ZeptoBars), so it is not a clean pin-for-pin OPA627 substitute. Check the pin function before op-amp rolling.
Noise is about 3x the OPA627's (ZeptoBars); ADI's LTspice model uses ~16 nV/rtHz.
Offset is higher than the OPA627's (0.5 mV vs 0.1 mV, per ZeptoBars).
Weaker headphone driver in Tangent's table (6.8 V needed for 0.5 V into 33 ohms).

counterfeit_notes: No fakes sold as AD744 were found. The hazard runs the other way: genuine AD744 dies have been remarked as OPA627. In April 2014 ZeptoBars decapped a cheap eBay DIP 'OPA627' (about $2 per Hackaday; $2.70 with shipping per the Habr text). It held an ADI AD744 die with only one laser-trimmed resistor, against several on a genuine metal-can OPA627. ZeptoBars thought a Chinese packager had bought AD744 dies or wafers; ADI's datasheet lists chip (die) form. The AD744's frequency-compensation feature was unused because the OPA627 has no matching pin. The 'AD'/'B744' die markings come from the Habr text and were not re-confirmed here. How to spot an AD744-based fake: (1) about 3x the noise and higher offset (0.5 mV vs 0.1 mV) than a genuine OPA627; (2) lower supply current, 3.5 mA for the AD744 (ADI datasheet) against about 7 mA for the OPA627 (TI figure, not re-checked here); (3) a decap. Discussed on Hackaday, Head-Fi and diyAudio ('more fake eBay semis (OPA627=AD744)'). Buy genuine AD744/AD746 through authorized distribution.
alternatives: ADI ADA4627-1 / ADA4625-1 / ADA4625-2 (modern low-noise JFET)
ADI AD711 / AD712 (slower BiFET siblings; ADI says the AD744 shares the AD711 family's DC performance)
TI OPA627 / OPA828 (Difet / JFET; buy genuine)

It is unknown which revisions the alldatasheet, datasheetcatalog, manualmachine and Octopart copies hold. Check them, and check Wayback copies of the static/imported-files URLs.

The datasheet values for noise (model 16 nV/rtHz), bias current and offset by grade are still model-derived.
No ADI die revision, fab move or PCN was found. It is unknown whether the 'B744' die mark means a mask revision.
Tangent's original English text on the AD744 was not retrieved.
The AD744 pin 8 (compensation) function versus OPA627 pin 8 has not been confirmed from a datasheet pinout.

corrections: The current ADI datasheet URLs are confirmed at /media/en/technical-documentation/data-sheets/ (ad744.pdf and AD746.pdf; both letter cases are indexed). They were only inferred before.
AD744 current datasheet revision: Rev. D (radiolocman mirror label). Rev. C is mentioned as older. The AD746 current revision is Rev. B (ADI product page, 8 pages).
Supply current is now datasheet-confirmed: AD744 3.5 mA, AD746 7 mA (it was model-derived).
GBW 13 MHz (internal compensation), 75 V/us slew and 500 ns settling to 0.01% for a 10 V step are now confirmed.
Grade definitions: C is an industrial (-40 to +85 C) grade and S/T are military grades. J/K are commercial.
AD746JRZ-REEL is obsolete (Digi-Key). The ad746.html product page is confirmed to exist; it was previously inferred.
The AD744 datasheet offers chip (die) form, which supports ZeptoBars' bare-die theory. Hackaday gives the fake's price as about $2 (the draft had $2.70, from the Habr text).
AD746 = two AD744 amplifiers on a single chip (ADI wording). ADI pitches the AD744 for audio with 0.0003% THD.

revision_chain_notes: Only Analog Devices made the AD744. No second sources or acquirer re-issues were found, so the chain is ADI 'REV.' letters only. The four searches did not show the Revision History table inside Rev. D, so the dates of Rev. C and Rev. D are still unknown. AD744 chain, oldest to newest: 1) Original edition(s), Rev. 0/A/B: MISSING. No copy or date found. The part existed by 1/91, when the SPICE macro-models were made, and those models include grades A/B/C/J/K/S/T. 2) Rev. C: a search summary says alldatasheet holds a 'REV.C' copy, but not which ID. Candidates are 48210, 48211 (AD744JN) and 553783. The Platan and Farnell copies are also probably Rev. C. The date is unknown. 3) Rev. D: current. Copies are on analog.com, radiolocman di=120133 (with ADI's 02/23/2017 quick-links page in front) and radiolocman di=171881. The date is unknown. The datasheet text lists five grades (J/K/A/B/T), but the 1991 models also had C and S grades, so a grade cull happened at an unknown revision. AD746 chain: 1) An edition dated 1995-10-31 (file date on the FindIC listing, low confidence), letter unknown, probably Rev. A or earlier. 2) Rev. B: current on analog.com, date unknown. Rev. 0 and Rev. A are MISSING. Still missing: every revision date, the contents of the Rev. D (AD744) and Rev. B (AD746) revision-history tables, a confirmed pre-Rev. C AD744 copy, and pre-Rev. B AD746 copies with visible letters. Next step: pull Wayback captures of the static/imported-files seeds (2008-2016), which probably hold Rev. C (AD744) and Rev. A or B (AD746). A 1990-1992 ADI Linear Products or Amplifier Reference databook scan would hold the original edition.
